name: Hotdata
license: Proprietary managed service; the CLI is MIT, and the DuckLake library it donated to DataFusion is Apache 2.0
summary: A managed SQL engine for AI agents, built in Rust on Apache DataFusion and Arrow: each agent gets short-lived “instant databases” to load data into, then runs read-only SQL, vector, full-text and geospatial queries over an HTTP API or CLI.
intro: Hotdata is a hosted query engine reached at `api.hotdata.dev`. An organization holds workspaces, and each workspace is an isolated execution environment that shares no compute, cache or credentials with any other. Inside it you create databases, lightweight query scopes made in one call that can delete themselves after an `expires_at` such as 24 hours; the intended pattern is one per job or per agent session. Data gets in two ways. You push files (CSV, JSON or Parquet) through an upload endpoint, where each publish atomically replaces, appends, upserts, updates or deletes rows by key. Or you set up ingests that pull from 168 source types in eight families: SQL databases and warehouses (Postgres, MySQL, SQL Server, Oracle, Snowflake, BigQuery, Databricks, Redshift), REST APIs, files in S3, GCS or Azure, Iceberg catalogs (REST, Glue, Polaris, Unity Catalog), Delta Lake, DuckLake, Kafka topics including Debezium change logs, and tables derived from other tables. A database can attach another database’s catalog read-only, so one query joins both, and since July 2026 it can be forked into an independent copy. Tables are stored with DuckLake through `datafusion-ducklake`, a library Hotdata wrote and donated to the DataFusion contrib project in June 2026.

SQL is read-only: `INSERT`, `COPY` and DDL are refused, and writes go through loads. The native dialect, HotSQL, is Postgres-like and built on DataFusion, and a query can instead be written in PostgreSQL, DuckDB or Snowflake syntax and translated before it runs. It adds BM25 full-text search, PostGIS-style `ST_` functions and vector search. Vector search runs on one node: an HNSW graph in USearch, scalar columns in SQLite and the full rows in Parquet, all sharing row keys. With a `WHERE` clause it first scans Parquet for matching keys, then either walks the graph with those keys as a filter (more than 5% of rows match) or computes exact distances for each key (5% or fewer). Long queries run asynchronously, and every result is saved and can be fetched again as Arrow, Parquet, CSV, Markdown or JSON.

The company was founded by Eddie A Tejeda (CTO), Divya Ranganathan (CEO) and Zac Farrell, with Andrew Lamb, PMC chair of Apache DataFusion, as an advisor. Its site went live in February 2026, the CLI in March and managed databases in May. Pricing is usage-based: a $5 monthly base fee, storage ($0.20 a month for 10 GB) and bytes scanned ($10.24 per TB), with a $100 credit at sign-up. The engine is closed source; the CLI, SDKs and integrations for Ibis, LangChain, dlt, dbt and Grafana are on GitHub.
strengths: Isolation by design: workspaces share nothing, databases are cheap to create, fork and expire, and attached catalogs are read-only, so many agents can work side by side without touching the sources
One SQL surface for analytics, BM25 full-text, filtered vector search and geospatial queries, and it accepts PostgreSQL, DuckDB and Snowflake dialects as well as its own
Pulls from 168 source types, from Postgres and Snowflake to Iceberg catalogs and Kafka, and saves every result so later steps can reuse it as data
In its own TPC-H benchmark (19 of 22 queries, July 2026), total execution time stayed between 2.59 and 2.90 s from 1 to 50 concurrent streams, while Snowflake rose from 2.88 to 9.26 s
limits: Very young: the site launched in February 2026 and managed databases in May 2026, and the closed-source engine is available only as Hotdata’s service

No write SQL at all: data arrives only through loads and ingests, the first load into a table must replace it, row-at-a-time writes are discouraged, and whether append and keyed loads work depends on how the instance is provisioned
Built for small, fast data, not warehouse scans: its founders target datasets under about 100 GB, and vector search runs on a single node sized for 1 to 10 million vectors

Its benchmark numbers are vendor-run: TPC-H Q18 failed on Hotdata at every concurrency level, and Q20 and Q21 were left out of the totals because more than about half their runs failed under concurrency

snippet.title: Load a Parquet file into an instant database, query it, search it, then delete it (from the Quick Start; not run, it needs a Hotdata account)
source: hotdata auth login                      # opens a browser to sign in
# An instant database with one declared table, loaded from a URL
hotdata databases create --name airbnb --catalog airbnb --table listings
hotdata query "SELECT count(id) AS total_rows FROM airbnb.public.listings"
# A BM25 full-text index on one column, then a search against it
hotdata search "cozy apartment with a view" \
# Throw the database away when the job is done

story: Hotdata comes from a bet that AI agents use data differently from people. In “Why we are building Hotdata” (April 2026), Eddie A Tejeda argued that a decade of infrastructure had optimized for throughput and scale, while vectorized execution, columnar formats, SIMD and fast NVMe let one machine process tens of millions of rows in under 10 ms. Agents, Tejeda wrote, create many datasets, issue large numbers of small queries and chain the results, so latency, context and composability matter more than raw throughput. A follow-up post added that one slow query can stall dozens of dependent steps in an agent’s plan.

The team built the engine on Apache DataFusion, a Rust query engine library, because it leaves storage, catalogs, indexing and caching to the builder. The engine’s caching layer landed in January 2026, the public site and geospatial SQL in February, the CLI with BM25 and vector search in March, and managed databases with automatic expiry in May. For table metadata it chose DuckLake over Iceberg: in June 2026 it released `datafusion-ducklake` to the DataFusion contrib organization and made it Hotdata’s storage backend. In July it added database forks and mutable tables and published a concurrency benchmark against Snowflake and BigQuery.

choices.choice: Build on DataFusion instead of a finished database
choices.why: Tejeda wrote that DuckDB is a complete database, while DataFusion provides planning, optimization and execution but lets the builder decide how data is stored, indexed, cached and planned, which is the control Hotdata wanted.

choices.choice: DuckLake instead of Iceberg for table metadata
choices.why: Reading an Iceberg table means walking metadata files, manifest lists and manifests in object storage before touching data. DuckLake keeps that metadata in a SQL database, so one query finds the Parquet files, which suits small, fast queries.

choices.choice: Vector search as a SQL operator, not a separate service
choices.why: Inspired by pgvector, the team wanted `WHERE` filters and `ORDER BY l2_distance(…) LIMIT k` in one query, aiming for under 100 ms with filters. It keeps three stores keyed alike (USearch, SQLite, Parquet) and picks a strategy from the filter’s selectivity.

choices.choice: Short-lived, isolated databases with durable results
choices.why: Agents lose their place when intermediate results disappear or change between runs, so every result is saved and replayable, and each job gets its own database that can expire on its own.

timeline.text: January: the caching layer lands, and query results become queryable data
February: hotdata.dev goes live, with geospatial SQL
March: the CLI launches, with BM25 full-text and vector search
June: `datafusion-ducklake` is donated to DataFusion contrib and becomes the storage backend
July: database forks, mutable tables and a concurrency benchmark
